claim: G-quadruplexes (G4) are alternative nucleic acid structures involved in transcription, translation and replication.
source: G-quadruplexes (G4) are alternative nucleic acid structures involved in transcription, translation and replication.
evidence: This is a general statement about G4 structures supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Aberrant G4 formation and stabilisation is linked to genome instability and cancer.
source: Aberrant G4 formation and stabilisation is linked to genome instability and cancer.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: G4 ligand treatment disrupts key biological processes leading to cell death.
source: G4 ligand treatment disrupts key biological processes leading to cell death.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the G4 field.

claim: This study presents the first unbiased genome-wide study to systematically identify human genes that promote cell death when silenced by shRNA in the presence of G4-stabilising small molecules.
source: To discover genes and pathways involved with G4s and gain mechanistic insights into G4 biology, we present the first unbiased genome-wide study to systematically identify human genes that promote cell death when silenced by shRNA in the presence of G4-stabilising small molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting the WEE1 cell cycle kinase in combination with G4 ligand treatment enhances cell killing.
source: We find that targeting the WEE1 cell cycle kinase or USP1 deubiquitinase in combination with G4 ligand treatment enhances cell killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing synergistic cell killing with WEE1 inhibitor and G4 ligand combinations.

claim: Targeting the USP1 deubiquitinase in combination with G4 ligand treatment enhances cell killing.
source: We find that targeting the WEE1 cell cycle kinase or USP1 deubiquitinase in combination with G4 ligand treatment enhances cell killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing synergistic cell killing with USP1 inhibitor and G4 ligand combinations.

claim: DDX42 DEAD-box helicase is a newly discovered G4-binding protein.
source: We also identify new genes and pathways regulating or interacting with G4s and demonstrate that the DDX42 DEAD-box helicase is a newly discovered G4-binding protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing DDX42 binding to G4 structures in ELISA assays.

claim: Over 700,000 G4s have been detected in vitro in the human genome.
source: In the human genome, over 700,000 G4s have been detected in vitro (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chambers et al., 2015.

claim: Sequences encoding G4s are enriched in regulatory regions consistent with roles in transcription and RNA regulation.
source: Sequences encoding G4s are enriched in regulatory regions consistent with roles in transcription and RNA regulation (Huppert and Balasubramanian, 2007; Huppert, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huppert and Balasubramanian, 2007 and Huppert, 2008.

claim: G4s are over-represented in oncogene promoters, such as MYC, KRAS and KIT.
source: their over-representation in oncogene promoters, such as MYC, KRAS and KIT, suggests that they are important in cancer and are potential therapeutic targets (reviewed in Balasubramanian et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balasubramanian et al., 2011.

claim: Computationally predicted G4s have been linked to replication origins.
source: Computationally predicted G4s have also been linked to replication origins (Besnard et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Besnard et al., 2012.

claim: Computationally predicted G4s have been linked to telomere homeostasis.
source: Computationally predicted G4s have also been linked to replication origins (Besnard et al., 2012) and telomere homeostasis (reviewed in Neidle, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Neidle, 2010.

claim: More than 3000 mRNAs have been shown to contain G4 structures in vitro, particularly at 5' and 3' UTRs.
source: In the transcriptome, more than 3000 mRNAs have been shown to contain G4 structures in vitro, particularly at 5' and 3' UTRs, suggestive of roles in posttranscriptional regulation (Bugaut and Balasubramanian, 2012; Kwok et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bugaut and Balasubramanian, 2012 and Kwok et al., 2016.

claim: G4-specific antibodies have been used to visualise G4s in protozoa.
source: G4-specific antibodies have been used to visualise G4s in protozoa (Schaffitzel et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schaffitzel et al., 2001.

claim: G4-specific antibodies have been used to visualise G4s in mammalian cells.
source: G4-specific antibodies have been used to visualise G4s in protozoa (Schaffitzel et al., 2001) and mammalian cells (Biffi et al., 2013; Henderson et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biffi et al., 2013; Henderson et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016.

claim: More G4s are detected in transformed versus primary cells.
source: More G4s are detected in transformed versus primary cells, and in human stomach and liver cancers compared to non-neoplastic tissues, supporting an association between G4 structures and cancer (Biffi et al., 2014; Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biffi et al., 2014 and Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016.

claim: More G4s are detected in human stomach and liver cancers compared to non-neoplastic tissues.
source: More G4s are detected in transformed versus primary cells, and in human stomach and liver cancers compared to non-neoplastic tissues, supporting an association between G4 structures and cancer (Biffi et al., 2014; Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biffi et al., 2014 and Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016.

claim: ChIP-seq was used to map endogenous G4 structure formation in chromatin revealing a link between G4s, promoters and transcription.
source: More recently, ChIP-seq was used to map endogenous G4 structure formation in chromatin revealing a link between G4s, promoters and transcription (Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016.

claim: G4s are found predominately in nucleosome-depleted chromatin within promoters and 5' UTRs of highly transcribed genes.
source: G4s are found predominately in nucleosome-depleted chromatin within promoters and 5' UTRs of highly transcribed genes, including cancer-related genes and regions of somatic copy number alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Several helicases, including WRN, BLM, PIF1, DHX36 and RTEL1, have been shown to unwind G4-structures in vitro.
source: Several helicases, including WRN, BLM, PIF1, DHX36 and RTEL1, have been shown to unwind G4-structures in vitro (Brosh, 2013; Mendoza et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brosh, 2013 and Mendoza et al., 2016.

claim: Fibroblasts from Werner (WRN) and Bloom (BLM) syndrome patients show altered gene expression that correlates with sites with potential to form G4s.
source: it is notable that fibroblasts from Werner (WRN) and Bloom (BLM) syndrome patients, who are predisposed to cancer, show altered gene expression that correlates with sites with potential to form G4s (Damerla et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Damerla et al., 2012.

claim: G4 ligands, such as pyridostatin (PDS), PhenDC3 and TMPyP4, can reduce transcription of many genes harbouring a promoter G4, including oncogenes such as MYC, in multiple cancer cell lines.
source: G4 ligands, such as pyridostatin (PDS), PhenDC3 and TMPyP4, can reduce transcription of many genes harbouring a promoter G4, including oncogenes such as MYC, in multiple cancer cell lines (Halder et al., 2012; McLuckie et al., 2013; Neidle, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halder et al., 2012; McLuckie et al., 2013; Neidle, 2017.

claim: G4-stabilising ligands interfere with telomere homeostasis by inducing telomere uncapping/DNA damage through the inhibition of telomere extension by telomerase leading to senescence or apoptosis.
source: G4-stabilising ligands also interfere with telomere homeostasis by inducing telomere uncapping/DNA damage through the inhibition of telomere extension by telomerase leading to senescence or apoptosis (reviewed in Neidle, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Neidle, 2010.

claim: 5' UTR RNA G4 structures may be involved in eIF4A-dependent oncogene translation.
source: 5' UTR RNA G4 structures may also be involved in eIF4A-dependent oncogene translation (Wolfe et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wolfe et al., 2014.

claim: Stabilisation of 5' UTR RNA G4 structures by G4-ligands can inhibit translation in vitro.
source: 5' UTR RNA G4 structures may also be involved in eIF4A-dependent oncogene translation (Wolfe et al., 2014) and their stabilisation by G4-ligands can inhibit translation in vitro (Bugaut and Balasubramanian, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bugaut and Balasubramanian, 2012.

claim: Several RNA G4-interacting proteins have been identified, including DEAD/DEAH helicases such as DDX3X and DHX36.
source: Identification of several RNA G4-interacting proteins (reviewed in Cammas and Millevoi, 2016), including DEAD/DEAH helicases such as DDX3X, and DHX36 (Chen et al., 2018; Herdy et al., 2018) additionally suggests specific roles for G4 structures in RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cammas and Millevoi, 2016; Chen et al., 2018; Herdy et al., 2018.

claim: Some G4-stabilising ligands cause a DNA damage-response (DDR).
source: Some G4-stabilising ligands cause a DNA damage-response (DDR); for example, DNA damage sites induced by PDS in human lung fibroblasts mapped to genomic regions at G4s within several oncogenes including SRC (Rodriguez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodriguez et al., 2012.

claim: Homologous recombination (HR) repair deficiencies can be exploited to selectively kill BRCA1/2-deficient cancer cells with G4 ligands.
source: Subsequent studies demonstrated that homologous recombination (HR) repair deficiencies can be exploited to selectively kill BRCA1/2-deficient cancer cells with G4 ligands (McLuckie et al., 2013; Zimmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLuckie et al., 2013 and Zimmer et al., 2016.

claim: CX-5461, a G4 ligand, has been applied to BRCA1/2-deficient breast cancers and is currently in clinical trials.
source: Recently, this concept has been applied to BRCA1/2-deficient breast cancers using CX-5461, a G4 ligand currently in clinical trials (Xu et al., 2017) (NCT02719977 ClinicalTrials.gov).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2017 and a clinical trial identifier.

claim: PDS and PhenDC3 are chemically and structurally dissimilar, but each shows a broad specificity for different G4 structural variants.
source: We employed PDS and PhenDC3 as representative G4 ligands as these are chemically and structurally dissimilar, but each shows a broad specificity for different G4 structural variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about these ligands.

claim: PDS and PhenDC3 have been widely used as G4-targeting probes in biophysical and biological studies.
source: Both ligands have been widely used as G4-targeting probes in biophysical (De Cian et al., 2007b; Rodriguez et al., 2008) and biological studies in which they have been shown to impart transcriptional inhibition, telomere dysfunction and replication stalling (De Cian et al., 2007a; Halder et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Cian et al., 2007b; Rodriguez et al., 2008; De Cian et al., 2007a; Halder et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2016.

claim: An unbiased genome-wide shRNA screen was performed in A375 human melanoma cells to globally evaluate genetic vulnerabilities to G4-ligands.
source: An unbiased genome-wide shRNA screen was performed in A375 human melanoma cells to globally evaluate genetic vulnerabilities to G4-ligands and to identify genes and pathways involved with G4-structures (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The shERWOOD-Ultramir shRNA pLMN retroviral library comprises 132,000 shRNAs across 12 randomised pools targeting the protein coding genome, with an average of five optimised hairpins per gene.
source: We used the latest generation shERWOOD-Ultramir shRNA pLMN retroviral library, comprising 132,000 shRNAs across 12 randomised pools targeting the protein coding genome, with an average of five optimised hairpins per gene (Figure 2C) (Knott et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knott et al., 2014 and the description of the library.

claim: A375 melanoma cells are TP53 wild-type and driven by oncogenic BRAF (V600E) and CDKN2A loss.
source: A375 melanoma cells were used due to their rapid doubling, stable ploidy and success in other shRNA-dropout screens (Sims et al., 2011); they are TP53 wild-type and driven by oncogenic BRAF (V600E) and CDKN2A loss (Forbes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sims et al., 2011 and Forbes et al., 2015.

claim: 9509 (~7%) G4-ligand-specific hairpins were found to be depleted (FDR ≤ 0.05; log2 FC <0) in the genome-wide screen.
source: For the whole library, when individual shRNAs are considered 9509 (~7%) G4-ligand-specific hairpins (i.e. those not in DMSO) were found to be depleted (FDR ≤ 0.05; log2 FC <0, Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 843 G4 ligand-specific gene knockdowns not present in DMSO were identified when a minimum of either 50% or three shRNA hairpins were significantly depleted for that gene.
source: We then reasoned, for a gene knockdown to have compromised cell growth, that a minimum of either 50% or three shRNA hairpins should be significantly depleted for that gene (median log2 FC <0). This resulted in the identification of 843 G4 ligand-specific gene knockdowns not present in DMSO (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: 758 G4 sensitisers were identified as those having a median log2 FC ≤ −1.
source: We then denoted a more stringent preliminary list of 758 G4 sensitisers as those having a median log2 FC ≤ −1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The screen independently validated the known G4 sensitisers BRCA1/2, ATRX and HERC2.
source: It is reassuring that in this list we independently validated the known G4 sensitisers BRCA1/2, ATRX and HERC2 (McLuckie et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017; Zimmer et al., 2016; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLuckie et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017; Zimmer et al., 2016 and data in Figure 3D.

claim: Eight additional G4 sensitisers (ADAR, DHX36, DNA2, FUS, MCRS1, RECQL4, SF3B3 and XRN1) were uncovered from genes annotated with G4-related terms in the UniprotKB, Gene Ontology (GO) and G4IPDB databases.
source: For genes annotated with G4-related terms in the UniprotKB, Gene Ontology (GO) and G4IPDB databases (Mishra et al., 2016), an additional eight sensitisers (ADAR, DHX36, DNA2, FUS, MCRS1, RECQL4, SF3B3 and XRN1) were uncovered (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E and citation to Mishra et al., 2016.

claim: Text-mining with G4 search terms using PolySearch2 revealed 12 additional sensitisers including helicases (RTEL1), DDR components (CHEK1, RAD17), transcriptional proteins (POLR1A, CNBP) and replication factors (ORC1, RPA3, TOP1).
source: Text-mining with G4 search terms using PolySearch2 on PubMed abstracts and open access full texts (see Materials and methods; Liu et al., 2015b) revealed a further 12 sensitisers arising from our screen including helicases (RTEL1), DDR components (CHEK1, RAD17), transcriptional proteins (POLR1A, CNBP) and replication factors (ORC1, RPA3, TOP1) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3F and citation to Liu et al., 2015b.

claim: Five significant enriched KEGG pathway clusters (p<0.05) were uncovered within the 758 G4-sensitiser gene list: 'cell cycle', 'ribosome', 'spliceosome', 'ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis' and 'DNA replication'.
source: Within the total 758 G4-sensitiser gene list, we uncovered five significant enriched KEGG pathway clusters (p<0.05): 'cell cycle', 'ribosome', 'spliceosome', 'ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis' and 'DNA replication' (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 20 out of 45 enriched GO 'Biological Process' terms and all 'Molecular Function' terms were classified into DNA or RNA classifications.
source: To gain functional insights, enriched GO 'Biological Process' and 'Molecular Function' terms were determined (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 1) which showed 20 out of 45 of the former and all the latter terms into DNA or RNA classifications, consistent with PDS/PhenDC3 directly binding nucleic acid G4 targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Enrichments in helicase C-terminal domains, RNA recognition motifs including RRM, RBD and RNP domains, and DNA-binding domains including zinc fingers, bZIP motifs and HMG boxes were discovered when protein domains were considered using GENE3D and PFAM databases.
source: Furthermore, when protein domains were considered using GENE3D and PFAM databases (Figure 4C), we discovered enrichments in helicase C-terminal domains, RNA recognition motifs including RRM, RBD and RNP domains, and DNA-binding domains including zinc fingers, bZIP motifs and HMG boxes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Enrichments in multifunctional ATPase domains and in ubiquitin hydrolase domains were found.
source: Consistent with the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis KEGG cluster, enrichments in multifunctional ATPase domains and in ubiquitin hydrolase domains, were also found.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of protein domains.

claim: Of the 758 sensitisers, there was a two-fold enrichment (p=9.1×10−6) for 50 cancer-associated genes in the COSMIC database.
source: Of the 758 sensitisers, there was a two-fold enrichment (p=9.1×10−6) for 50 cancer-associated genes, which increases to three-fold (p=2.5×10−3) when considering only sensitisers common to both G4 ligands (Figure 5A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A, 5B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: STRING network analysis revealed a DDR cluster that included BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as their interacting tumour suppressor partners PALB2 and BAP1.
source: Notably, when STRING network analysis (Szklarczyk et al., 2017) was used to investigate functional interactions, this revealed a DDR cluster that included BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as their interacting tumour suppressor partners PALB2 and BAP1, two cancer-associated DDR genes not previously indicated as G4 ligand sensitisers. (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5C and citation to Szklarczyk et al., 2017.

claim: A cluster consisting of several chromatin modifiers including SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and SMARCE1 was identified as sensitisers.
source: This analysis also identified as sensitisers a cluster consisting of several chromatin modifiers including SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and SMARCE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by STRING network analysis data.

claim: A custom shRNA screening panel was developed encompassing the gene sensitisers identified in the genome-wide screen plus additional G4-associated genes noted from the literature.
source: To enable more rigorous and further comparative analyses that focus solely on G4 sensitisers, we developed a custom shRNA screening panel encompassing the gene sensitisers identified above plus additional G4-associated genes noted from the literature (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the custom panel and Figure 6A.

claim: The custom panel consisted of a single retroviral shRNA pool with 8018 shRNAs.
source: This panel consisted of a single retroviral shRNA pool to allow all shRNAs to be screened simultaneously under standardised conditions and to minimise technical fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the custom panel in the Materials and methods.

claim: Using the custom panel with A375 melanoma cells with PDS and PhenDC3, 342 G4 sensitisers were recovered corresponding to 40.6% overlap (308 genes) with the complete genome-wide screen.
source: Using A375 melanoma cells with PDS and PhenDC3, the custom panel recovered a total of 342 G4 sensitisers corresponding to 40.6% overlap (308 genes) with the complete genome-wide screen (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: 290 G4 sensitisers were identified with 89 and 161 unique for PDS and PhenDC3, respectively, and 40 genes common for both ligands.
source: From this, we identified 290 G4 sensitisers with 89 and 161 unique for PDS and PhenDC3, respectively, and 40 genes common for both ligands (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 27 out of 40 sensitiser genes common between PDS and PhenDC3 associated with DNA or RNA binding processes, such as chromatin modification, replication transcription, and translation.
source: We next considered that the 40 sensitiser genes common between PDS and PhenDC3 reflected the most robust sensitisers for G4 ligands in general and it is notable that 27 out of 40 associated with DNA or RNA binding processes, such as chromatin modification, replication transcription, and translation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: 74 G4-sensitisers were found in the classifications 'Druggable Genome' and 'Clinically Actionable' within the druggable genome interaction database (DGIdb) with 13 being common to both classifications.
source: A total of 74 G4-sensitisers were found in the classifications 'Druggable Genome' (genes with known or predicted drug interactions) and 'Clinically Actionable' (genes used in targeted clinical cancer sequencing for precision medicine) with 13 being common to both classifications (Figure 6G, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 12 genes within DGIdb were found among the 40 most robust sensitisers common to both G4 ligands, including 5 (BRCA1, CHEK1, CDK12, TOP1, PDKP1) common to both druggable and clinically actionable classifications.
source: Performing a similar analysis on the 40 most robust sensitisers common to both G4 ligands gave 12 genes within DGIdb (Figure 6H, Supplementary file 1), including 5 (BRCA1, CHEK1, CDK12, TOP1, PDKP1) common to both druggable and clinically actionable classifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The custom HT1080 screen recovered a total of 121 G4 ligand sensitisers, with the majority (73 genes, 58%) shared with those seen for each ligand in the A375 genome-wide screen.
source: The custom HT1080 screen recovered a total of 121 G4 ligand sensitisers, with the majority (73 genes, 58%) shared with those seen for each ligand in the A375 genome-wide screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the HT1080 screen.

claim: Cytoscape network analysis revealed a core set of G4-associated genes/pathways for these genes in spliceosome, HR and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis processes (p<0.0005).
source: Cytoscape network analysis (Figure 7A) revealed a core set of G4-associated genes/pathways for these genes in spliceosome, HR and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis processes (p<0.0005).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: 29 PDS and 22 PhenDC3 gene sensitivities were found to be shared across all three screens.
source: Overall, 29 PDS and 22 PhenDC3 gene sensitivities were found to be shared across all three screens (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Four genes were repeatedly found as G4 ligand sensitisers- BRCA1, TOP1, DDX42 and GAR1, as they consistently appeared in both cell types and with both G4-ligands in all screens.
source: When we evaluated the data collectively from all screens, it was apparent that four genes were repeatedly found as G4 ligand sensitisers- BRCA1, TOP1, DDX42 and GAR1, as they consistently appeared in both cell types and with both G4-ligands in all screens (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: siRNA knockdown of BRCA1, TOP1, DDX42 and GAR1 in HT1080 cells imparted significant increases in sensitivity with PDS or PhenDC3 compared to DMSO.
source: Mirroring the shRNA screen findings, siRNA knockdown of all four genes in HT1080 cells imparted significant increases in sensitivity with PDS or PhenDC3 compared to DMSO.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA validation experiments described in the text.

claim: Synergy was found for both PDS and MK1775 or pimozide combinations in HT1080 cells.
source: In HT1080 cells, synergy was found for both PDS and MK1775 or pimozide combinations (Figure 9C,D, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with peak synergies of 21% and 24% at 156 nM PDS with 21 nM MK1775 or 6.25 μM pimozide, respectively (GI50 for PDS, MK1775 and pimozide alone = 322 nM, 59 nM and 8.4 μM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9C, 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A375 cells showed lower synergy with PDS and MK1775 combination with peak synergy of 15% at 8 μM PDS, 444 nM MK1775.
source: A375 cells showed lower synergy with PDS and MK1775 combination (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), with peak synergy of 15% at 8 μM PDS, 444 nM MK1775 (GI50 for PDS, MK1775 and pimozide alone = 8.5 μM, 625 nM and 12.2 μM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greatest synergy was seen in combinations of PDS and pimozide in A375 cells with a peak synergy of 61% at 5.33 μM PDS, 6.25 μM pimozide.
source: The greatest synergy was seen in combinations of PDS and pimozide in A375 cells (Figure 9F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with a peak synergy of 61% at 5.33 μM PDS, 6.25 μM pimozide.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Long-term clonogenic survival assays revealed a similar potentiation of growth inhibition for PDS/MK1775 and PDS/pimozide drug combinations for both cell lines tested.
source: Furthermore, long-term clonogenic survival assays revealed a similar potentiation of growth inhibition, albeit at lower compound concentrations, for PDS/MK1775 and PDS/pimozide drug combinations for both cell lines tested (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: DHX36 and DHX9 are known G4 helicases.
source: Indeed, DHX36 and DHX9, known G4 helicases (Giri et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Chakraborty and Grosse, 2011; Creacy et al., 2008 ; Vaughn et al., 2005) and the DEAD box protein DDX3X, that was recently shown to bind RNA G4s (Herdy et al., 2018), were identified as G4 sensitisers in our screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Giri et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Chakraborty and Grosse, 2011; Creacy et al., 2008; Vaughn et al., 2005.

claim: DDX3X was recently shown to bind RNA G4s.
source: Indeed, DHX36 and DHX9, known G4 helicases (Giri et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Chakraborty and Grosse, 2011; Creacy et al., 2008 ; Vaughn et al., 2005) and the DEAD box protein DDX3X, that was recently shown to bind RNA G4s (Herdy et al., 2018), were identified as G4 sensitisers in our screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herdy et al., 2018.

claim: DDX42 is a non-processive RNA helicase.
source: DDX42 is a non-processive RNA helicase (Uhlmann-Schiffler et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uhlmann-Schiffler et al., 2006.

claim: DDX42 has been associated with splicing.
source: DDX42 is a non-processive RNA helicase (Uhlmann-Schiffler et al., 2006) and has been associated with splicing (Will et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Will et al., 2002.

claim: DDX42 predominantly localises to the nucleus (~4 to 9-fold greater than cytoplasmic levels) in three independent cell lines, (HT1080, HEK293 and HeLa).
source: By immunoblotting of nuclear and cytoplasmic sub-cellular fractions (Figure 10B–E), we first established that DDX42 predominantly localises to the nucleus (~4 to 9-fold greater than cytoplasmic levels) in three independent cell lines, (HT1080, HEK293 and HeLa).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10B-E.

claim: DDX42 bound the NRAS G4 folded in KCl with an apparent Kd of 71.1 ± 3.5 nM.
source: DDX42 bound the NRAS G4 folded in KCl with an apparent Kd of 71.1 ± 3.5 nM and did not bind detectably to the mutant oligonucleotide or RNA hairpin controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data described in the text.

claim: DDX42 did not bind detectably to the mutant oligonucleotide or RNA hairpin controls.
source: DDX42 bound the NRAS G4 folded in KCl with an apparent Kd of 71.1 ± 3.5 nM and did not bind detectably to the mutant oligonucleotide or RNA hairpin controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data described in the text.

claim: DDX42 binds to the MYC DNA G4 with an apparent Kd of 232.9 ± 23.5 nM with little binding to the mutant control.
source: DDX42 affinity by ELISA (Figure 10G) showed that DDX42 binds to the MYC DNA G4 with an apparent Kd of 232.9 ± 23.5 nM with little binding to the mutant control.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 10G.

claim: The G4 sensitiser screen has enabled identification and classification of DDX42 as a G4-interacting protein as a new finding.
source: Thus, the G4 sensitiser screen has enabled us to identify and classify DDX42 as a G4-interacting protein as a new finding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing DDX42 binding to G4 structures.
